title: A tide service and harbour groundings
bodyMd: In the decade after the harbour authority of Varrow replaced its printed tide tables with a free telephone service announcing the predicted tide every hour, the number of fishing boats that ran aground in the harbour fell by nearly a third. The authority cites the figure as proof that the service has made the harbour safer. Yet in the same decade the main channel was dredged so deep that most boats can no longer touch bottom there even at low water, and the service's own logs show that fewer than one call in ten came from a working fishing vessel. The authority's inference is therefore premature, though not, on the evidence available, false: what the figures cannot yet show is whether the boats that stopped running aground were the ones whose skippers called.
accessibilityText: A one-paragraph passage. The authority cites this as proof that the service has made the harbour safer. Yet in the same decade the main channel was dredged so deep that most boats can no longer touch bottom there even at low water, and the service's own logs show that fewer than one call in ten came from a working fishing vessel. The author concludes that the authority's inference is premature, though not, on the evidence available, false, because the figures cannot yet show whether the boats that stopped running aground were the ones whose skippers called.

provenance.notes: Original short argument passage written for wave 7 to carry two Reading Comprehension questions. The port of Varrow, its tide service, the grounding figures, the dredging and the call logs are all invented. The author's verdict is deliberately qualified (premature but not shown false) so that questions can test the difference between undermining an inference and refuting its conclusion. Not taken from or modelled on any ETS passage.
